questions.stem: A charge of 12 C passes a point in a wire in 4.0 s. What is the current?
questions.explanation: I = q/t = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A. One ampere is one coulomb per second. Multiplying the charge by the time gives 48, and dividing time by charge gives 0.33.

questions.stem: A current of 0.50 A flows through a lamp for 1.0 minute. Using e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, how many electrons pass through the lamp?
questions.explanation: The charge is q = It = 0.50 × 60 = 30 C, and dividing by the charge on one electron gives 30/1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.9 × 10²⁰ electrons. Using 1.0 s instead of 60 s gives 3.1 × 10¹⁸, and 30 is the charge in coulombs, not a number of electrons.

questions.stem: In a circuit connected to a battery, which way do conventional current and electrons flow through the external circuit?
options: Conventional current flows from negative to positive; electrons flow from positive to negative
Both flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the battery
Both flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of the battery
Conventional current flows from positive to negative; electrons flow from negative to positive
questions.explanation: Conventional current was defined as the flow of positive charge, from the positive terminal round to the negative terminal. In metal wires the charge carriers are electrons, which move the opposite way, from negative to positive.

questions.stem: Why do free electrons drift along a metal wire when it is connected across a battery?
options: The battery releases electrons into the wire, which travel at the speed of light to the far end
The battery's magnetic field attracts electrons along the wire towards its positive terminal
The metal ions in the wire move towards the negative terminal and push the electrons along
The potential difference sets up an electric field in the wire that pushes on the free electrons
questions.explanation: The potential difference across the wire creates an electric field inside it. The field exerts a force on the free (delocalised) electrons, giving them a slow net drift opposite to the field, which is the current. The metal ions stay fixed in the lattice.

questions.stem: How does alternating current (AC) differ from direct current (DC)?
options: AC flows only in parallel circuits; DC flows only in series circuits
AC is carried by protons; DC is carried by electrons
AC reverses its direction many times a second; DC always flows in one direction
AC always flows in one direction; DC reverses its direction many times a second
questions.explanation: In AC, the charge carriers oscillate back and forth as the current reverses direction periodically; Australian mains supply completes 50 cycles each second (50 Hz). In DC, from a battery for example, the current flows one way only. Both are carried by electrons in metal wires.

questions.stem: The potential difference across a resistor of constant resistance is doubled. What happens to the current through it?
questions.explanation: With R constant, V = IR means current is directly proportional to voltage, so doubling V doubles I. A larger voltage gives each coulomb more energy and drives charge through faster.

questions.stem: Two wires have the same length and thickness, one of copper and one of nichrome. The nichrome wire has a much higher resistance. Which factor explains the difference?
options: The cross-sectional area of the wire
The material the wire is made of
questions.explanation: The length and cross-sectional area are the same, so the difference comes from the material: nichrome resists the flow of electrons much more than copper does. This is why copper is used for connecting wires and nichrome for heating elements.

questions.stem: A 2.0 m length of resistance wire has a resistance of 4.0 Ω. What is the resistance of a 5.0 m length of the same wire?
questions.explanation: Resistance is proportional to length for a wire of the same material and thickness: 4.0 × (5.0/2.0) = 10 Ω. Electrons collide with more of the lattice over a longer path. Inverting the ratio gives 1.6 Ω.

questions.stem: A wire is replaced by one of the same material, twice as long and with twice the cross-sectional area. How does its resistance compare?
options: It is four times as large
questions.explanation: Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Doubling the length doubles R, and doubling the area halves it, so the two changes cancel.

questions.stem: A wire is replaced by one of the same material and length but half the diameter. What happens to its resistance?
options: It becomes a quarter as large
It becomes four times as large
questions.explanation: The cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so halving the diameter makes the area a quarter as large. Since resistance is inversely proportional to area, it becomes four times as large. Doubling would follow if R depended on the diameter directly.

questions.stem: Why does the resistance of a metal wire increase when its temperature rises?
options: The metal loses free electrons to the air around it as it is heated
The metal ions vibrate more, so the free electrons collide with them more often
The free electrons slow down and stop moving once they are heated
The wire becomes thinner, as metals contract when they are heated
questions.explanation: At higher temperatures the positive ions in the lattice vibrate with larger amplitude, so drifting electrons collide with them more often, which hinders the current. Metals expand slightly when heated, they do not contract.

questions.stem: What current flows through a 12 Ω resistor with 6.0 V across it?
questions.explanation: From V = IR, I = V/R = 6.0/12 = 0.50 A. Multiplying gives 72, and dividing the resistance by the voltage gives 2.0.

questions.stem: In an experiment, a graph of current (y-axis) against voltage (x-axis) for a resistor is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 0.040 A V⁻¹. What is the resistance?
questions.explanation: The straight line through the origin shows the resistor is ohmic. With current on the y-axis, the gradient is I/V = 1/R, so R = 1/0.040 = 25 Ω. Reading the gradient as the resistance gives 0.040 Ω.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an ohmic conductor from a non-ohmic one?
options: Its resistance is zero, so any voltage drives an unlimited current
Its current is directly proportional to the voltage, so its resistance is constant
Its current is inversely proportional to the voltage, so its resistance is constant
Its resistance always increases as the current through it increases
questions.explanation: An ohmic conductor obeys Ohm's law: at constant temperature, I is directly proportional to V, giving a straight-line I-V graph through the origin. A non-ohmic conductor, such as a filament lamp, has a resistance that changes with the current.

questions.stem: The current-voltage graph for a filament lamp curves, with its gradient getting smaller as the voltage increases. What does this show?
options: The lamp is non-ohmic, and its resistance decreases as the filament heats up
The lamp is ohmic, and its resistance increases as the filament heats up
The lamp is non-ohmic, and its resistance increases as the filament heats up
The lamp is ohmic, and its resistance stays constant as the filament heats up
questions.explanation: Each increase in voltage produces a smaller increase in current, so V/I rises: the resistance increases. A larger current heats the filament, and a hotter metal has a higher resistance. A curved graph means the lamp does not obey Ohm's law.

questions.stem: A filament lamp draws 0.40 A at 2.0 V and 0.80 A at 6.0 V. How does its resistance change between these voltages?
options: It rises from 5.0 Ω to 10 Ω
It rises from 5.0 Ω to 7.5 Ω
It falls from 7.5 Ω to 5.0 Ω
questions.explanation: R = V/I at each point: 2.0/0.40 = 5.0 Ω and 6.0/0.80 = 7.5 Ω. The value 10 Ω comes from the gradient between the two points (4.0 V/0.40 A), but resistance is the ratio V/I at a point, not the slope of the graph.

questions.stem: An electric heater runs on 240 V and draws a current of 10 A. What is its power?
questions.explanation: P = VI = 240 × 10 = 2400 W. Power is the rate at which electrical energy is transformed, here into thermal energy. Dividing the voltage by the current gives 24, which is the heater's resistance in ohms.

questions.stem: A kettle transforms 2.4 × 10⁵ J of electrical energy into thermal energy in 2.0 minutes. What is its power?
questions.explanation: P = ΔE/Δt = 2.4 × 10⁵/120 = 2000 W. Leaving the time in minutes gives 1.2 × 10⁵ W, and multiplying energy by time gives 4.8 × 10⁵.

questions.stem: How much electrical energy does a 60 W lamp transform in 2.0 hours?
questions.explanation: ΔE = PΔt = 60 × 2.0 × 3600 = 4.32 × 10⁵ J. The time must be in seconds. Using 2.0 for the time gives 120 J, and 7.2 × 10³ is the time in seconds, not an energy.

questions.stem: A current of 5.0 A flows through a cable with a resistance of 2.0 Ω. At what rate is energy lost as heat in the cable?
questions.explanation: P = I²R = 5.0² × 2.0 = 50 W. Forgetting to square the current gives 10 W. This loss is why transmission lines carry electricity at high voltage and low current.

questions.stem: The current through a resistor is doubled while its resistance stays the same. By what factor does the power dissipated change?
options: It becomes four times as large
questions.explanation: P = I²R, so power is proportional to the square of the current. Doubling I multiplies P by 2² = 4.

questions.stem: A 12 V supply drives a current of 2.0 A through a small electric motor. The motor delivers 18 W of mechanical power. At what rate is energy lost as heat and sound in the motor?
questions.explanation: The electrical power input is P = VI = 12 × 2.0 = 24 W. By conservation of energy, the 24 W in equals the 18 W of useful mechanical output plus the losses, so 24 − 18 = 6.0 W is lost as heat and sound.

questions.stem: How are ammeters and voltmeters connected in a circuit?
options: Ammeters in parallel with a component; voltmeters in series with it
Both in series with the component being measured
Both in parallel with the component being measured
Ammeters in series with a component; voltmeters in parallel with it
questions.explanation: An ammeter measures the current through a component, so that current must pass through the meter: it goes in series. A voltmeter compares the energy per coulomb at two points, so it connects across the component, in parallel.

questions.stem: Why should a voltmeter have a very high resistance?
options: So it adds a large resistance in series and protects the circuit from damage
So the full current flows through it and its reading is as large as possible
So it converts the potential difference into a current that it can measure
So it draws almost no current and barely changes the circuit it is measuring
questions.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel. If its resistance were low, a significant current would flow through it, changing the currents and voltages it is meant to measure. An ammeter, connected in series, should instead have a very low resistance.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between connecting lamps in series and in parallel?
options: In series each lamp gets the full supply voltage; in parallel the lamps share the voltage
In series the lamps share one path for current; in parallel each lamp is on its own branch
In series each lamp is on its own branch; in parallel the lamps share one path for current
In series the current divides between the lamps; in parallel it is the same in each lamp
questions.explanation: A series circuit has a single path, so the same current flows through every lamp and they share the supply voltage. A parallel circuit has separate branches, each connected across the supply, so each lamp gets the full voltage and the current divides.

questions.stem: Three lamps are connected in series. One lamp's filament breaks. What happens?
options: All three lamps go out, because the only path for the current is broken
Only the broken lamp goes out, because the others are on separate branches
The other two lamps glow brighter, because the current through them increases
The other two lamps stay the same, because the current is shared between them
questions.explanation: In a series circuit there is only one path, so a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. In a parallel circuit each lamp is on its own branch, so the others would stay lit. This is why household lights are wired in parallel.

questions.stem: What is the total resistance of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω resistors connected in series?
questions.explanation: In series, R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 Ω. The current passes through each resistor in turn, so their resistances add. Using the parallel formula gives about 5.5 Ω.

questions.stem: Resistors of 2.0 Ω, 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω are connected in series to a 24 V supply. What are the current and the voltage across the 4.0 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: The total resistance is 12 Ω, so I = 24/12 = 2.0 A, the same through every resistor in series. The voltage across the 4.0 Ω resistor is V = IR = 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 V. The 6.0 A comes from using the full 24 V across the 4.0 Ω resistor alone.

questions.stem: Why do the voltages across components in a series circuit add up to the supply voltage?
options: The current is used up as it passes through each component in turn around the loop
Each component receives the full supply voltage, which is then shared at the end
Conservation of energy: each coulomb uses up all the energy per coulomb the supply gave it
Conservation of charge: each coulomb leaving the supply must return to the supply
questions.explanation: Voltage is energy per coulomb. The supply gives each coulomb a certain energy, and by conservation of energy all of it is transformed in the components around the loop, so V = V₁ + V₂ + ... Conservation of charge explains why current is the same throughout a series loop; current is not used up.

questions.stem: What is the total resistance of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor connected in parallel?
questions.explanation: 1/R = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 1/6.0 + 2/6.0 = 3/6.0, so R = 2.0 Ω. The combined resistance of a parallel group is always less than the smallest resistor in it. Stopping at 1/R gives 0.50.

questions.stem: A 4.0 Ω and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. What is the current drawn from the supply?
questions.explanation: Each branch has the full 12 V across it: I₁ = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A and I₂ = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A. The total current is the sum, 5.0 A. Adding the resistances as if in series gives 12/10 = 1.2 A.

questions.stem: Why is the total current in a parallel circuit equal to the sum of the currents in the branches?
options: The branches each have the same resistance, so the current splits equally
The voltage divides between the branches, and the currents add to match
Conservation of charge: charge entering a junction must equal charge leaving it
Conservation of energy: each coulomb uses up all its energy in the branches
questions.explanation: Charge is not created or destroyed, so every coulomb per second arriving at a junction must leave along the branches: I = I₁ + I₂ + ... The branches need not have equal resistances; the current divides in inverse proportion to them.

questions.stem: A third resistor is connected in parallel with two resistors already in parallel across a battery. What happens to the circuit's total resistance and the current from the battery?
options: Total resistance decreases and the battery current increases
Total resistance increases and the battery current decreases
Total resistance decreases and the battery current decreases
Total resistance increases and the battery current increases
questions.explanation: Each extra parallel branch provides another path for charge, so the total resistance falls and, with the same voltage, more current flows from the battery. The current in each existing branch is unchanged, since each still has the full battery voltage across it.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are connected to the same battery, first in series and then in parallel. How does the brightness of each lamp compare?
options: Each lamp has the same brightness in both circuits, because the lamps are identical
Each lamp is brighter in the parallel circuit, because the current through each is halved
Each lamp is brighter in the parallel circuit, because each has the full battery voltage
Each lamp is brighter in the series circuit, because the same current flows through both
questions.explanation: In series the two lamps share the battery voltage, so each has half of it and a smaller current. In parallel each lamp has the full voltage across it, so more current flows through each and each transforms more power, glowing brighter.

questions.stem: A 10 Ω resistor is connected in series with two 10 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: The parallel pair has 1/R = 1/10 + 1/10, so R = 5.0 Ω. Adding the 10 Ω in series gives 15 Ω. Treating all three as in series gives 30 Ω.

questions.stem: A 4.0 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 12 Ω resistors, all connected to a 16 V supply. What is the current through the 12 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: The parallel pair is 1/(1/6.0 + 1/12) = 4.0 Ω, so the total is 8.0 Ω and the supply current is 16/8.0 = 2.0 A. The pair has 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 V across it, so the 12 Ω resistor carries 8.0/12 ≈ 0.67 A; the other 1.3 A goes through the 6.0 Ω resistor.

questions.stem: In an experiment on a combination circuit, the measured supply current is slightly less than the value calculated from the labelled resistances and the supply voltage. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: The ammeter has a very high resistance, which is needed so that it does not disturb the circuit
Charge is lost from the circuit as it passes through the resistors, so less returns to the supply
The voltmeter connected in parallel adds extra resistance in series with the rest of the circuit
The supply's internal resistance and the connecting wires add resistance not included in the calculation
questions.explanation: Real supplies have internal resistance and real wires have some resistance, so the total resistance is a little higher than calculated and the current a little lower. Resistor tolerances also contribute. Charge is conserved, an ammeter should have a very low resistance, and a voltmeter in parallel does not add series resistance.

questions.stem: Two identical resistors are connected to the same supply, first in series and then in parallel. How does the total power drawn from the supply in parallel compare with that in series?
questions.explanation: Two equal resistors R give 2R in series and R/2 in parallel, so the parallel resistance is one-quarter of the series value. With the same supply voltage, P = VI = V²/R, so the power in parallel is four times as large.
